newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN DLR HOLDS ITS GROUND, BUT NOT YET SAFE.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN DLR HOLDS ITS GROUND, BUT NOT YET SAFE.

text.p: The Australian dollar caught its breath on Monday after having moved away from two-year lows reached last week, but remained vulnerable to further losses.
The unit held to a tight range on the day, finding support at US$0.7350 but lacking the concerted buying needed to take it through resistance starting at around US$0.7370.
"It's making all these moves offshore and doing nothing in our time" said Dresdner's director of treasury, Rob Hollonds.
By 4.30 p.m. (0630 GMT) the dollar was at US$0.7362/67, up from an early US$0.7352/57 and half a cent above Friday's close of US$0.7311/16.

Most interest in the region was centred on the U.S. dollar, which had a choppy day after falling heavily in New York on Friday. The U.S. dollar was trading at 1.8461.66 marks and 115.05/10 yen from New York closes of 1.8450/60 and 114.75/85.
That fed through to the Australian dollar, with traders saying most were default moves caused by the changes in the U.S. dollar rather than outright cross trading.
At 4.30 p.m (0630 GMT). the Australian dollar was at 84.72/82 yen and 1.3588/3605 marks, up on an early 84.32/42 and 1.3568/81, but still down on Friday's late 86.51/61 and 1.3633/46.

The dollar had gained half a cent on Friday night, taking it away from the two-year lows reached on Friday, after the gold price improved and there was some reported switching out of Canadian dollar assets.

While trade was subdued on Monday, with the market waiting on a speech by Reserve Bank governor Ian Macfarlane on Tuesday and a raft of U.S. data through the week, traders said the dollar retained a downside bias.
"I think the market's expecting the Aussie to trade a range, and see what Macfarlane's got to say in Perth tomorrow," Hollonds said.

It will be Macfarlane's first public speech since the July 30 rate cut -- in fact it will be his first speech in Australia since before the May 23 rate cut -- and his words will be examined for clues to the interest rate outlook.
The rate cuts that have been delivered, and the prospect that there could be more, have been the key factor behind the five month downtrend from the 1997 high of US$0.80 in March.

"The reality of life with the Aussie is that nobody wants to seem to buy the thing strategically, it's too expensive to buy and given the traditional buyers are not being paid to hold long Aussie anymore, they just won't come in there," Hollonds said.
Macfarlane's speech on the topic of monetary policy and growth, while keenly waited, will do little to allay the complaints of traders that most of the moves happen offshore.

The speech is being delivered at a dinner function in Perth, which because of time differences, means he will start talking at around 11.00 p.m. Sydney time -- or 1300 GMT, which is during afternoon European trading.
